paragraphs: Combining fMRI measurements from several people helps researchers assess whether a finding extends across individuals. However, aligning brain anatomy does not necessarily align brain function: corresponding anatomical locations can have different functional roles across people. This paper develops a reduced-dimension shared response model that accounts for those differences when combining datasets.

The central task is to identify a response shared across subjects while allowing their functional topographies to differ. This matters because a common response need not appear in exactly the same anatomical pattern for everyone. The model therefore addresses a source of variation that anatomical alignment alone does not resolve.

Across several datasets and brain regions, the model improves sensitivity to shared responses. Removing the identified common response also improves detection of differences between groups. These findings give the model two related uses: studying what participants have in common and making differences easier to detect after accounting for that common component.
neurips-2015-a-reduced-dimension-fmri-sh.tldr: A shared response model combines fMRI data across people while accounting for functional differences, improving detection of common responses and group differences.

paragraphs: When regression predicts several outputs, the noise in those outputs can have a shared covariance structure. Maximum likelihood estimation accounts for that structure and can be substantially more accurate than ordinary least squares. The difficulty is computational: obtaining the maximum likelihood estimate generally involves a non-convex optimization problem without a known efficient general solution.

The paper studies this tradeoff for pooled regression and seemingly unrelated regression. It provides upper and lower estimation-error bounds for finite samples, moving beyond comparisons that describe only what happens as the amount of data grows indefinitely. These bounds identify specific situations in which accounting for noise covariance produces a substantial accuracy advantage.

For both models, an efficient alternating minimization procedure achieves the same performance guarantee as maximum likelihood estimation up to universal constants. The analysis also covers high-dimensional settings, where the procedure improves on corresponding least-squares solutions and has an error bound depending only logarithmically on dimensionality. The contribution connects statistical advantages to a computationally practical procedure.
neurips-2015-alternating-minimization-fo.tldr: Efficient alternating minimization matches maximum likelihood error guarantees up to constants in two multiple-output regression models.

paragraphs: Information spreading through a network can undergo a transition from limited propagation to a super-critical cascade. This paper studies both the influence of an initial set of nodes and the timing of that transition in continuous-time diffusion. These questions connect how widely a contagion spreads with when its behavior changes.

The authors introduce the Laplace Hazard matrix and show that its spectral radius characterizes influence and explosion-time dynamics in the diffusion processes they study. This supplies a mathematical link between a matrix associated with the process and its spreading behavior. Using that link, they derive tight influence bounds that do not rely on an asymptotic limit.

The paper also formally defines critical explosion time, develops tight lower bounds for it, and examines the point after which contagion becomes super-critical. Examples drawn from epidemiology and viral marketing illustrate the theory. Numerical experiments across different network types support the tightness of the bounds, connecting the mathematical analysis to observed cascade behavior.
neurips-2015-anytime-influence-bounds-an.tldr: The Laplace Hazard matrix links continuous-time cascade influence and explosion timing to a spectral quantity, enabling tight theoretical bounds.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural-network prediction accounts for uncertainty about model parameters when predicting an output. This can matter when data are scarce or when applications such as bandits and active learning need accurate predictive distributions. Monte Carlo methods offer one approach, but they require storing many parameter samples and making predictions with many versions of the network.

The paper proposes compressing that collection of predictions into a single deep neural network. Its target is the Monte Carlo approximation to the posterior predictive distribution: the output distribution obtained by accounting for parameter uncertainty. Distillation makes this predictive information available in a more compact form, reducing the need to retain and evaluate many separate models.

The authors compare their method with Bayesian neural-network approaches based on expectation propagation and variational Bayes. They report better performance, simpler implementation, and less computation at prediction time in those comparisons. The contribution is a way to make approximate Bayesian prediction more economical by learning a single network to represent the sampled models' predictive behavior.
neurips-2015-bayesian-dark-knowledge-ae8.tldr: Bayesian dark knowledge distills Monte Carlo predictive distributions into one neural network, reducing storage and prediction costs.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization searches for a function's optimum using evaluations rather than an explicit formula. Here, those evaluations contain noise, and the function can have any dimension. The paper assumes local smoothness around at least one global optimum, but the optimizer does not know that smoothness in advance.

The proposed algorithm, parallel optimistic optimization, or POO, adapts to this missing information. Its purpose is to approach the performance of algorithms that receive the smoothness information beforehand. This matters because the theoretical properties needed to configure an optimization method may themselves be unavailable when the only access to a function is through noisy evaluations.

A finite-time analysis bounds POO's error after n evaluations within a factor of sqrt(ln n) of the best known methods that know the smoothness. The authors also establish applicability to a broader function class, including functions they characterize as difficult to optimize. The result quantifies the cost of adaptation while retaining the stated local-smoothness assumption.
neurips-2015-black-box-optimization-of-n.tldr: POO optimizes noisy functions with unknown local smoothness, with a finite-time error guarantee close to methods that know the smoothness.

paragraphs: This paper develops a model for generating natural images by organizing generation across multiple scales. It uses a Laplacian pyramid and a cascade of convolutional networks to build images from coarse structure toward finer detail. The approach gives image generation a sequence of scale-specific stages.

Each pyramid level has its own generative convolutional network trained with the generative adversarial network approach. The overall model therefore combines adversarial learning with a coarse-to-fine organization. The architectural idea matters because the generation process explicitly separates scales while combining their contributions into a finished image.

The authors report substantially improved sample quality relative to existing models. In a human evaluation, generated CIFAR10 images were mistaken for real images around 40% of the time, compared with 10% for GAN samples. They also present samples from STL10 and LSUN, which contain more diverse images. The human assessment provides a concrete perceptual comparison, while those additional samples illustrate the model's application beyond the dataset used for that reported measurement.
neurips-2015-deep-generative-image-model.tldr: A Laplacian pyramid of adversarial convolutional networks generates images from coarse to fine, improving reported perceptual sample quality.

paragraphs: Disease measurements can be noisy and collected at uneven intervals. Continuous-time hidden Markov models accommodate both features, describing progression through hidden states between observations. Their usefulness has been restricted by difficult parameter learning, which previously limited models to small state spaces or required unrealistic constraints on how states could change.

The paper organizes efficient expectation-maximization learning around two separate calculations. One estimates the probabilities of hidden states given the observations. The authors reformulate this calculation as an equivalent discrete-time hidden Markov model whose transitions vary with time. The other computes statistics conditioned on endpoint states, using three methods adapted from continuous-time Markov chain research.

This separation gives a complete characterization of efficient EM-based learning methods for these models. The authors demonstrate models with more than 100 states on glaucoma and Alzheimer's disease datasets, using them to visualize and predict progression. The demonstrations show that the learning approach supports substantially richer state descriptions while retaining a model suited to irregular, noisy observations.
neurips-2015-efficient-learning-of-conti.tldr: Efficient EM learning enables continuous-time hidden Markov disease models with more than 100 states for irregular, noisy observations.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning uses relationships between prediction tasks to help them learn together. An output kernel represents those relationships as a matrix. Learning this matrix alongside the tasks avoids requiring users to specify it, but enforcing its positive semidefinite structure can require an eigendecomposition at every optimization step, making many-task problems expensive.

The paper shows that, for a particular class of regularizers, explicitly imposing the positive semidefinite constraint is unnecessary. The relaxed problem automatically satisfies it. This qualification is central: the result identifies a useful class of formulations in which the structural requirement is preserved even after removing the explicit constraint.

That observation leads to an unconstrained dual optimization problem that can be solved efficiently. Experiments on several multi-task and multi-class datasets demonstrate computational efficiency and generalization performance. The practical significance is that learning task relationships need not always carry the repeated matrix-decomposition cost associated with directly enforcing the kernel constraint, provided the regularizer belongs to the class covered by the result.
neurips-2015-efficient-output-kernel-lea.tldr: For a specified class of regularizers, output-kernel learning can drop an explicit matrix constraint and use an efficient unconstrained dual formulation.

paragraphs: The Jaccard index measures similarity between pairs of data samples. Missing observations make those similarities difficult to estimate, and errors accumulate across the matrix of pairwise comparisons. This paper begins with a Jaccard matrix approximated from incomplete data and improves it by enforcing structural requirements on the matrix.

The proposed calibration uses alternating projections to satisfy positive semidefiniteness and other constraints. Its focus is the similarity matrix itself, whereas conventional approaches first fill in missing data and then calculate similarities. Enforcing matrix-level requirements gives the method a direct way to improve the object that subsequent learning tasks will use.

The authors prove that calibration brings the matrix closer to the unknown true matrix in Frobenius norm, except for special cases where calibration leaves it unchanged. This guarantee compares the calibrated estimate with its uncalibrated starting point. Empirical experiments support the theoretical result, and benchmark learning tasks show significantly improved outcomes. Together, these findings connect a matrix-level error guarantee to practical benefits in downstream learning.
neurips-2015-estimating-jaccard-index-wi.tldr: Calibrating an incomplete-data Jaccard matrix to satisfy structural constraints improves its Frobenius-distance accuracy, except when it remains unchanged.

paragraphs: Empirical risk minimization chooses a model by minimizing loss on observed data. The statistical question is how close that model's expected loss comes to the best achievable expected loss. This paper studies that question for smooth, exp-concave losses, a framework covering important problems such as regression, squared-hinge-loss classification, and portfolio selection.

Under this framework, the authors show that empirical risk minimization achieves an expected-loss convergence rate of d/n, where d is the dimension and n is the sample size. The rate makes the dependence on both quantities explicit: the guarantee improves with more observations and accounts for the number of dimensions being learned.

The bound matches existing lower bounds up to constant factors and removes a logarithmic factor from the previous state of the art. Earlier guarantees were associated with converting computationally expensive online algorithms into batch predictors. The contribution establishes that ERM itself can attain the faster statistical rate for the stated loss class, strengthening the theoretical case for this direct learning principle.
neurips-2015-fast-rates-for-exp-concave-.tldr: For smooth, exp-concave losses, empirical risk minimization achieves a d/n generalization rate that matches lower bounds up to constants.

paragraphs: Multidimensional recurrent neural networks have performed well in speech and handwriting recognition, and increasing their depth can improve sequence labeling. Training becomes harder as these networks deepen. This paper investigates Hessian-free optimization as a way to overcome that learning difficulty and make deeper multidimensional recurrent networks usable.

A central obstacle comes from connectionist temporal classification, or CTC, the learning objective used for sequence labeling. Its non-convexity creates a problem when applying Hessian-free optimization. The authors formulate a convex approximation to CTC and discuss how this approximation relates to the expectation-maximization algorithm and the Fisher information matrix.

Using the resulting approach, they successfully train a multidimensional recurrent network with up to 15 layers and report improved sequence-labeling performance. The contribution links greater model depth to an optimization method adapted to the particular training objective. The convex approximation addresses the identified obstacle in applying Hessian-free learning; the reported training result demonstrates that the combined approach can support substantially deeper networks.
neurips-2015-hessian-free-optimization-f.tldr: A convex approximation to CTC enables Hessian-free training of multidimensional recurrent networks up to 15 layers, improving sequence labeling.

paragraphs: A probabilistic predictor attaches probabilities to possible outcomes, making the reliability of those probabilities part of the learning problem. This paper studies a computationally efficient way to turn machine-learning algorithms into probabilistic predictors with a theoretical validity property described as perfect calibration. The method is examined both theoretically and empirically.

The guarantee comes with a tradeoff: the predictor returns imprecise probabilities rather than a single precise probability. In practice, the authors find that this imprecision becomes very small for large datasets. This means the guaranteed form can become almost precise empirically while still retaining the distinction between an imprecise output and one exact probability.

The paper also considers merging the imprecise outputs into precise probabilities. That step loses the theoretical perfect-calibration property, but the resulting predictors consistently outperform existing methods in the reported empirical accuracy studies. The two versions therefore offer different supported benefits: one retains a formal validity guarantee, while the merged version provides precise outputs with favorable observed accuracy.
neurips-2015-large-scale-probabilistic-p.tldr: An efficient predictor conversion guarantees perfect calibration with imprecise probabilities; merging them yields strong empirical accuracy but loses that guarantee.

paragraphs: Large neural networks demand substantial memory and computation, which can make embedded deployment difficult. Conventional training adjusts weights within a fixed architecture. This paper also changes which connections remain, using training to identify a smaller network that preserves the predictive accuracy of the original in the reported experiments.

The method has three stages. First, the full network is trained so that the importance of its connections can be assessed. Next, unimportant connections are removed. Finally, the remaining weights are retrained to adapt the reduced network. This final adjustment is part of the method, so the resulting network reflects both connection selection and further weight learning.

On ImageNet, AlexNet's parameter count falls from 61 million to 6.7 million, a ninefold reduction, with no reported accuracy loss. VGG-16 falls from 138 million to 10.3 million parameters, a thirteenfold reduction, again without accuracy loss. These results demonstrate substantial redundancy in the tested networks and support learning connectivity as a way to reduce neural-network resource requirements.
neurips-2015-learning-both-weights-and-c.tldr: Training, pruning, and retraining reduce AlexNet and VGG-16 parameter counts by 9× and 13× without reported accuracy loss.

paragraphs: In multi-label prediction, some possible outputs are naturally closer to one another than others. A learning objective can use that relationship instead of treating all output differences alike. This paper develops a loss based on Wasserstein distance, which measures dissimilarity between probability measures using a chosen metric on the output space.

Exact Wasserstein optimization is costly, so the authors build an efficient learning algorithm around a regularized approximation. They also extend the distance to unnormalized measures, broadening the kinds of output representations it can compare. A statistical learning bound provides theoretical support for the proposed loss alongside the computational method.

The Wasserstein loss can encourage predictions to vary smoothly with respect to the selected output metric. On a tag-prediction task using the Yahoo Flickr Creative Commons dataset, the approach outperforms a baseline that does not use that metric. The result demonstrates a practical benefit of incorporating output relationships into training, with the chosen metric supplying the structure that the loss uses.
neurips-2015-learning-with-a-wasserstein.tldr: A regularized Wasserstein loss incorporates relationships between labels into efficient learning and improves a reported image-tag prediction task.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix completion reconstructs a matrix from a limited set of observed entries. This paper addresses two linked problems: determining the rank from few randomly revealed entries and obtaining a reconstruction with small error. Knowing the rank matters because it describes the size of the low-rank structure being recovered.

The proposed MaCBetH algorithm uses the Bethe Hessian matrix. It estimates rank by counting negative eigenvalues, then uses the corresponding eigenvectors to initialize a procedure that minimizes disagreement with observed entries. The spectral calculation thus supplies both a structural estimate and a starting point for fitting the missing-data reconstruction.

In a random-matrix setting, the authors use results from the statistical mechanics of Hopfield networks to analyze detection. They show efficient rank detection for a large n-by-m matrix from C(r)r sqrt(nm) entries, with C(r) close to one. Empirical root-mean-square reconstruction errors compare favorably with existing approaches. The theoretical detection result and empirical reconstruction assessment support different parts of the algorithm's purpose.
neurips-2015-matrix-completion-from-fewe.tldr: MaCBetH uses Bethe Hessian eigenvalues to estimate matrix rank and eigenvectors to initialize accurate low-rank completion.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient MCMC methods support Bayesian learning on large datasets, but their behavior depends on how their dynamics are numerically integrated. This paper develops convergence theory for general SG-MCMC methods using higher-order integrators. It studies both finite-run estimation error and the invariant distributions associated with their long-run behavior.

The theory shows faster convergence and more accurate invariant measures with higher-order integration. For the proposed second-order symmetric splitting integrator, SGHMC posterior-average mean squared error achieves an optimal rate of L^(-4/5) over L iterations. The corresponding rate for SGHMC and SGLD using first-order Euler integration is L^(-2/3), giving a concrete theoretical improvement.

The authors also analyze decreasing step sizes. For a particular decreasing sequence, these methods attain the same convergence rates as their fixed-step-size counterparts. Synthetic and real-data experiments support the theoretical analysis, with advantages demonstrated in two large-scale applications. The work establishes numerical integration order as a consequential design choice for both convergence speed and the accuracy of approximate Bayesian sampling.
neurips-2015-on-the-convergence-of-stoch.tldr: Higher-order integrators improve SG-MCMC convergence guarantees, including an L^(-4/5) posterior-average MSE rate for the proposed SGHMC integrator.

paragraphs: The paper asks how many observations are needed to choose k high-mean distributions from n unknown candidates, allowing a small relative error under the selection criterion. The goal is efficient selection, so the number of samples matters as well as the quality of the chosen set.

Two observation settings are considered. In the multi-armed bandit setting, each distribution can provide arbitrarily many independent, identically distributed samples. In the hidden bipartite graph setting, each distribution comes from a finite population of size m and becomes completely known after m samples. This difference changes what additional sampling can reveal and therefore matters to the selection problem.

For each setting, the authors prove lower bounds on the total number of samples any solution needs and present algorithms whose sample complexities match those bounds. The matching results establish optimal sampling efficiency for the studied formulations. Treating both settings makes clear how optimal selection depends on whether observations come from an indefinitely sampleable distribution or an exhaustible finite population.
neurips-2015-on-top-k-selection-in-multi.tldr: Matching sampling lower bounds and algorithms establish optimal approximate top-k selection in bandit and finite-population graph settings.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups similar items together and separates dissimilar items using a similarity graph. KwikCluster provides a three-approximation guarantee, but its sequential neighborhood-clustering process can require many rounds. This paper introduces two parallel algorithms, C4 and ClusterWild!, designed to remove that scaling bottleneck on large graphs.

C4 controls concurrency so that the parallel process remains serializable, preserving the three-approximation guarantee. ClusterWild! removes coordination to improve scaling, accepting a provably small degradation of that approximation ratio. Both algorithms use a polylogarithmic number of rounds and have theoretical guarantees of nearly linear speedups. Their different coordination choices expose a concrete tradeoff between consistency and parallel efficiency.

Experiments report improvements over the state of the art in clustering accuracy and running time. The authors demonstrate clustering billion-edge graphs in under five seconds on 32 cores, with a fifteenfold speedup. These results show that the parallel formulations can translate their theoretical scaling properties into substantial practical gains on very large graph instances.
neurips-2015-parallel-correlation-cluste.tldr: C4 and ClusterWild! parallelize correlation clustering with approximation guarantees and demonstrated billion-edge processing in under five seconds.

paragraphs: Gibbs sampling often works well empirically for inference on factor graphs, yet its theoretical behavior can be poor. Even a tree-shaped graph can have a mixing time that grows exponentially with the number of variables. The paper seeks a structural property that gives a more useful guarantee about how quickly Gibbs sampling approaches its target distribution.

The authors introduce hierarchy width, a property of graphs and hypergraphs. They prove that bounded hierarchy width ensures polynomial mixing time when the factor weights satisfy suitable conditions. The guarantee depends on both requirements, connecting graph structure and weights to sampling efficiency rather than relying on tree structure alone.

The analysis is partly motivated by hierarchical factor-graph templates, whose hierarchy width stays bounded regardless of the data used to instantiate them. That makes the property useful at the model-template level. In a natural-language-processing application, the authors establish rapid mixing and report accuracy exceeding human volunteers. The application combines a formal sampling guarantee with strong observed task performance.
neurips-2015-rapidly-mixing-gibbs-sampli.tldr: Bounded hierarchy width, together with suitable weight conditions, guarantees polynomial-time mixing for Gibbs sampling on factor graphs.

paragraphs: Many learning objectives combine a data-fitting loss with a regularization penalty, and both components can be nonsmooth. In high dimensions, classical proximal-gradient approaches with smoothing can become impractical because they require a proximal operator at every iteration. This paper proposes a first-order method for handling such composite optimization problems.

Semi-Proximal Mirror-Prox treats the objective's parts through different operations. It uses a saddle-point representation for one part and linear minimization over the domain for the other. This arrangement provides a way to work with the composite structure when repeatedly computing the proximal operations required by more classical methods would be costly.

The authors establish a convergence rate with optimal complexity bounds for the number of calls to a linear minimization oracle. That guarantee concerns a specific computational resource: how often the algorithm must solve its linear minimization subproblem. Experiments provide promising comparisons with competing methods. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support this combination of saddle-point optimization and linear minimization for high-dimensional nonsmooth objectives.
neurips-2015-semi-proximal-mirror-prox-f.tldr: Semi-Proximal Mirror-Prox combines saddle-point methods and linear minimization with optimal linear-oracle complexity for nonsmooth composite optimization.

paragraphs: Text categorization assigns documents to categories such as sentiment or topic. This paper develops a semi-supervised convolutional neural-network framework that uses unlabeled text to learn representations before integrating them into supervised classification. Its key choice is to represent small regions of text, extending the learned unit beyond individual words.

The region embeddings are learned through a scheme based on two-view semi-supervised learning. The aim is to make representations learned without labels useful for the eventual classification task. These embeddings are then incorporated into a supervised CNN, linking information extracted from unlabeled text with learning from labeled examples.

The authors report better results than previous approaches on sentiment and topic classification. These findings support learning representations at the level of text regions as a useful component of the tested categorization models. The contribution brings together the choice of representation unit, a learning scheme intended to preserve task-relevant information without labels, and integration into a supervised network; the reported gains concern that overall framework.
neurips-2015-semi-supervised-convolution.tldr: Learning text-region embeddings from unlabeled data improves supervised CNN results on reported sentiment and topic classification tasks.

paragraphs: Many learning tasks require choosing a small subset of variables that still performs well. Feature selection, sparse regression, and dictionary learning all involve versions of this problem. The paper proposes POSS, an approach that uses evolutionary Pareto optimization to address the competing goals of subset size and predictive performance.

The Pareto perspective treats compactness and performance as separate objectives to be considered together. This gives the search a way to pursue small, effective subsets while accounting for the tradeoff between those goals. The paper's theoretical analysis focuses on sparse regression, where it proves that POSS efficiently attains the best approximation guarantee available in the stated comparison.

For the Exponential Decay subclass, the authors establish the stronger result that POSS reaches an optimal solution. That exact-optimality claim applies to the named subclass. Empirical studies support the theoretical findings and show better performance than greedy and convex-relaxation methods in the reported evaluations. The contribution combines a multi-objective search strategy with problem-specific approximation and optimality guarantees.
neurips-2015-subset-selection-by-pareto-.tldr: POSS uses evolutionary Pareto optimization for compact variable selection, with sparse-regression approximation guarantees and exact optimality for an Exponential Decay subclass.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a Bayesian interpretation of plasticity in spiking neural networks. Inherent randomness in synaptic change is treated as a mechanism for sampling possible synaptic parameters from a posterior distribution. Under this view, ongoing variability can participate in probabilistic inference rather than simply disappearing as learning progresses.

The framework offers an alternative to models in which synaptic weights converge to maximum likelihood estimates. It explains how prior preferences over weight distributions and connection probabilities can be combined optimally with learned experience. Both connection strengths and the probability of connections therefore enter the account of how a network adapts.

In simulations, the proposed plasticity model lets spiking networks continually compensate for unforeseen disturbances. The authors also present it as a normative mathematical framework for understanding persistent variability and rewiring in brain networks. The distinction between proposal and evidence matters: the paper supplies a probabilistic explanation and simulation results showing adaptive behavior, with those results supporting the framework's viability as an account of plasticity.
neurips-2015-synaptic-sampling-a-bayesia.tldr: Synaptic sampling models plasticity as Bayesian posterior sampling and shows continuous compensation for unexpected disturbances in spiking-network simulations.

paragraphs: A way to evaluate machine reading is to ask questions about documents a system has seen. Training and testing such systems requires substantial supervised data connecting documents with questions and answers. This paper identifies the lack of large-scale datasets for this purpose as a bottleneck and introduces a methodology for providing that data.

The data contribution enables the authors to develop attention-based deep neural networks for reading comprehension. These networks learn to read real documents and answer complex questions with minimal prior knowledge of language structure. The approach connects a scalable source of supervision with a model class designed for the document-question task.

The significance lies in addressing the data and learning problems together. The methodology supplies the examples needed for large-scale supervised training and evaluation, while the networks demonstrate what can be learned from that supervision. The stated result concerns document-based question answering, giving a concrete setting in which reading behavior can be trained and assessed rather than leaving comprehension as an unmeasured goal.
neurips-2015-teaching-machines-to-read-a.tldr: A methodology for large-scale reading-comprehension data enables attention-based networks to answer complex questions about real documents.

paragraphs: This paper builds a model of natural textures using the internal features of convolutional neural networks trained for object recognition. The starting network was trained for a discriminative task, yet its learned feature spaces also support generating perceptually convincing textures. The work demonstrates a generative use for representations learned through recognition.

Textures are represented through correlations between feature maps at several network layers. These correlations describe relationships among the network's responses and provide the model's account of texture. Across layers, the authors find that the representations increasingly capture natural-image statistics while also making information about objects more explicit.

Samples from the model have high reported perceptual quality, supporting the usefulness of these feature relationships for texture generation. The model also provides a tool for creating neuroscience stimuli. Beyond that practical application, the authors suggest it might help explain the deep representations learned by convolutional networks. This interpretive possibility is grounded in examining what the layerwise texture representations retain and reveal about images.
neurips-2015-texture-synthesis-using-con.tldr: Correlations among features in an object-recognition CNN support high-quality texture synthesis and offer a tool for studying learned representations.
